opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a slightly awkward position for me to be in, because I'm one of the people who helped create the thing I'm now complaining about. But I think that gives me some licence to say it.

When we wrote the transformer paper, the field was much more exploratory. People were trying recurrent architectures, convolutional ones, memory-augmented networks, all sorts of strange ideas. The transformer came out of that kind of freedom. Now it's worked so well that almost all the money, the compute, the talent and the attention have collapsed onto one recipe: take a transformer, scale it, add more data, do some post-training. Because that recipe keeps paying off, there's enormous pressure to just keep turning the crank.

That's what I mean by a local minimum. Gradient descent on research works the same way it does on a loss surface. If every step you take is the one that gives the most immediate improvement, you end up very good at being exactly where you are, and you lose the ability to see that there might be a much deeper valley somewhere else. To get there you'd have to go uphill for a while, try things that initially perform worse, and almost nobody is incentivised to do that right now. If you're a PhD student and you propose a genuinely new architecture, a reviewer will ask why it doesn't beat a huge transformer on some benchmark. Of course it doesn't, it hasn't had billions of dollars and years of engineering poured into it.

There's also a historical irony. Before transformers, recurrent networks were dominant, and a lot of people were making incremental tweaks to LSTMs. It took a step sideways to break out of that. I'd be surprised if the transformer were the final answer, and I worry that we're now so locked in that whatever comes next will be really hard to discover, because we've stopped looking.

So that's a big reason I've personally stepped back from transformer work. I'd rather spend my time on things like nature-inspired approaches, evolution, collective intelligence, open-endedness, ideas where you're explicitly searching for novelty rather than just optimising the thing you already have. Some of them will fail, but the field as a whole needs people willing to explore, or we'll just keep polishing the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrent networks had been dominant and that a sideways move broke out of incremental LSTM tweaks, but it does not state that switching to transformers produced a language-modeling improvement far larger than those tweaks.

r002.rationale: It compares pre-transformer LSTM tweaks with the move to transformers and says the field is now locked into one recipe. It does not clearly warn that small transformer refinements risk becoming obsolete after a future architectural breakthrough.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and it's a bit awkward for me to say, because I'm one of the people who helped build the thing that everyone's now obsessed with. But I genuinely think we're in a local minimum, and the reason is almost sociological rather than technical.

Think about what's happened over the last few years. The transformer worked really well, scaling it worked really well, and so an enormous amount of money and talent flooded into one very narrow direction. And when that happens, the incentives change completely. If you're a researcher now, the safe thing to do is take the architecture everyone's using, tweak it a bit, scale it a bit, get a slightly better number on a benchmark, and publish. You'll get the paper accepted, you'll get the job, you'll get the funding. Whereas if you go off and try something genuinely different, there's a very good chance it just won't work, and you'll have spent two years on it with nothing to show.

And the thing is, that's not how the transformer came about. We were a bunch of people in a very open research environment, we weren't under pressure to ship a product, and we were essentially allowed to mess around. Nobody told us we had to make it work. Quite a lot of what we tried didn't work. That freedom to explore was exactly what produced the breakthrough, and I look around now and I see a lot less of that freedom, ironically because of how successful the result was.

There's also the compute dimension. The frontier has become so expensive that the exploration that does happen tends to happen inside a handful of large labs, and those labs have very strong commercial reasons to keep pushing on what already works. So you get this feedback loop: the dominant paradigm attracts the resources, the resources make the dominant paradigm better, and everything else looks worse by comparison, not necessarily because it's a worse idea but because it's had a tiny fraction of the attention.

I should be clear, I'm not saying language models are a dead end or that they aren't useful. They obviously are. What I'm saying is that I don't think anyone really believes that this exact recipe, just bigger, is the whole story of intelligence. There are things about how these systems learn, how inefficient they are compared to a human child, how brittle they can be, that suggest there's something fundamental we haven't figured out yet. And my worry is that we've organised the entire field in a way that makes it very hard to go looking for it.

So part of what I'm trying to do now is recreate a little of that earlier environment. Give people room to be curious, to follow things that look interesting rather than things that look publishable, and accept that most of it will fail. Because the next big idea, if it's anything like the last one, probably won't come from optimising the thing we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers worked well and scaling attracted investment, but does not compare switching from RNNs with incremental RNN improvements or describe the improvement as far larger.

r002.rationale: It warns that optimizing the current recipe may miss the next big idea, but does not say small transformer refinements could become obsolete after a breakthrough, or compare that risk with RNN research after transformers arrived.

astra-6.text:
My worry is that we’ve found something that works extremely well, and that makes it harder to explore anything fundamentally different. If you’re starting a research project, improving a large language model is a fairly safe bet. You have an architecture, you have benchmarks, and you can make measurable progress. Trying a completely different idea might get you nowhere for a year.

So the incentives push everyone toward the same approach. And then you get this feedback loop: the tools, the hardware, the funding, and the way we evaluate research all become geared toward making that approach better. An alternative has to compete with something that’s had an enormous amount of engineering behind it before anyone takes it seriously.

That doesn’t mean language models are a dead end. I think they’re amazing. But making progress within a particular framework isn’t the same as knowing that it’s the best framework. We need room for people to follow ideas that look worse initially, because you sometimes have to go downhill before you can find a higher hill.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the appeal of improving large language models, but does not mention RNNs, transformers, or a comparison between architectural and incremental language-modeling gains.

r002.rationale: The response warns that research may overfocus on one framework, but does not say small transformer refinements could become obsolete after an architectural breakthrough or compare this to RNN refinements after transformers arrived.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, my worry is that we’ve found something that works so well that it’s become very difficult to justify working on anything else. If you can take an existing architecture, make it bigger, and get a fairly predictable improvement, that’s a very attractive research programme—especially if you’re a company trying to build a product.

But that changes the kinds of questions people ask. Instead of asking, “What are we missing about intelligence?” you start asking, “How do we make this model a little better?” Those are useful questions, but they’re a much narrower set of questions.

And there’s a feedback loop: the funding goes there, the compute goes there, the researchers go there, and then most of the progress we see comes from that direction. That can look like evidence that it’s the only promising direction, when it’s also partly a consequence of where we’re putting all our effort.

I don’t mean that language models have hit a wall. They could improve enormously. The concern is that there might be a different approach that initially looks worse, or doesn’t fit our benchmarks, but ultimately gets us somewhere these systems can’t. You need room for people to explore those ideas without having to beat a huge language model in their first paper.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention RNNs, transformers, or a language-modeling improvement from switching architectures.

r002.rationale: It warns that a different approach could eventually outperform language models, but does not say small transformer refinements could become obsolete or compare them with RNN refinements after transformers arrived.
